Version 3, shaped from Matthew’s feedback.
Start with one scene. Change the approach. Notice who, or what, gets your attention.

One problem: make a football game feel like football

A fictional design meeting prompted by Matthew’s Madden example. These are invented roles and lines, not a reconstruction of the Madden team’s conversations.

Choose how the room responds to difference
LIGHT THE SAME SCENE

Same people. Same needs. The fourth seat lets you see what the meeting is doing to the game.

01 / The room becomes a contest

“My version wins.”

  • Design“Keep it fast. Cut the football decisions. My version is easier to sell.”
  • Football“But reading the field is part of playing football.”
  • Engineering“I can build what was decided. That doesn’t mean we solved the problem.”
What gets made: a flashy scoring demo.

One voice becomes the specification. The game loses the judgment that makes football interesting.

02 / A yes conceals a no

“Fine. Whatever you want.”

  • Football“Every formation, every adjustment, in the first build.”
  • Design“Then new players will need a way into all that complexity.”
  • Engineering / spoken, then unspoken“Sure.”
    “We can’t build and test all of this in the time we have.”
What gets made: an unbuildable promise.

The silence sounds like agreement. A real constraint disappears from the conversation, but not from the work.

03 / The midpoint becomes the goal

“Let’s just meet halfway.”

  • Design“One simple play.”
  • Football“A full playbook.”
  • Engineering“Half a playbook, then. We can all give something up and finish this meeting.”
What gets made: half a playbook, no way in.

Less content has not solved learning, football judgment, or feasibility. Everyone loses something; no new idea appears.

04 / Difference becomes material

“What does the game need?”

  • Design contributes a way in“What if a new player learns through one short drive?”
  • Football contributes real judgment“Keep reading the defense. Two meaningful choices could teach that.”
  • Engineering contributes a test“One drive, two decisions, one prototype. We can build it and watch people play.”
What gets made: a playable learning drive.

Each contribution changes the idea. It is buildable, approachable, and still asks the player to think like a football player. Now test whether it works.

The people stay in place. Change the approach and notice what happens to their shared work.

The key image

Another presence.
A different question.

The thing at the fourth seat is not a person. But treating it as present changes what we owe the meeting.

Matthew reached for Madden: first football, then the game itself, as something larger than any individual at the table. Here, the fourth seat makes that shared work visible.

Instead of asking only “Did I get my way?”, try “What can exist now because these particular people worked on it together?”

A shared purpose does not erase power, rights, consent, or limits. Some decisions call for a clear no. Some practical compromises are useful. The failure shown above is splitting the difference without understanding what the work needs.

A way to change course

Notice. Ask. Make a move.

IF SOMEONE NEEDS TO WIN

Bring the work back.

“What are we trying to make possible? What does your proposal protect?”

Keep the need. Let the proposed solution change.

IF A YES GOES QUIET

Give the limit a voice.

“What haven’t we made room to say? What cannot be promised?”

Leave space to disagree, pass, or pause without penalty.

IF HALFWAY IS THE ANSWER

Try another shape.

“What could use both contributions? What small version would let us learn?”

A new possibility is a hypothesis, not proof of success.

Your table / two or more people

Give your work
a fourth seat.

Bring one unfinished idea. Let another person change it. Keep the original contributions visible so you can see whether something new actually happened.

Back to Matthew’s workshop

The people in the room
are the material.

The scene is a short invitation into the practice. Your own experiences and contributions carry the workshop.

PART 1

What are we doing here?

Name what you are making. Notice whether the room expects a contest, an exchange, or shared creation.

PART 2

What do we do with difference?

Try the three tempting approaches. Look for the contribution or constraint each one loses.

PART 3

How do we make a good table?

Practice in changing groups. Make one new possibility, keep what is unresolved visible, and choose a small test.

Before the workshop: four prompts, with room to pass

Matthew’s proposal begins with an anonymous pre-survey and live anonymous questions. This page collects nothing. These prompts can be used in a separately agreed anonymous process:

  1. When did someone change your thinking in a group?
  2. What helps you speak up, and what makes you hold back?
  3. What do you tend to do when people disagree?
  4. What distinguishes the best group you have been in from the worst?

A facilitator should agree how responses are handled before collecting them, invite people to pass, and avoid attributing anyone’s private experience without permission.

For Matthew: what this draft is testing

Your feedback asked us to show winning, acquiescing, and splitting the difference; carry over the cinema attention experiment; and give the thing being made a place at the table. This draft uses the same scene for all four approaches and lets the lighting turn toward the people or the work.

The dialogue and practice example are invented for discussion. The three workshop questions and Madden connection come from your outline and feedback. The fourth seat is a visual interpretation, not a claim that this is your finished method.

Three useful questions: Does the scene make the failure modes recognizable? Does the fourth seat change the question you ask? Where does the good outcome feel too neat, or need more difficulty?

Take this to your next table

“What are we making, and what can your difference help it become?”
